questions.q: How does the 'statistics' in this lesson differ from SET STATISTICS TIME/IO covered in T-SQL Development?
options: Column/index statistics are stored summaries of value distribution the optimizer reads before building any plan, unlike SET STATISTICS TIME/IO, which measures one query's runtime and page reads in a session
They are exactly the same feature under two different names
SET STATISTICS TIME/IO is what the optimizer uses to build execution plans
Column and index statistics only exist in Azure SQL Database, not on-premises
questions.explain: SET STATISTICS TIME/IO is session-scoped measurement of one execution; column/index statistics are persistent inputs the optimizer reads before planning every query.

questions.q: Why can stale statistics cause the optimizer to choose the wrong shape of plan, not just a slower version of the right one?
options: Because cardinality estimates come from statistics, not an actual row count, so a plan built around an outdated row-count guess (e.g. nested loop for 40 rows) can be catastrophic if the real count is now 400,000
Because stale statistics only ever add a fixed, small overhead to any plan
Because SQL Server refuses to run queries once statistics are older than 24 hours
Because plan shape is unrelated to cardinality estimates
questions.explain: A plan appropriate for 40 rows and one appropriate for 400,000 rows are structurally different plans, not the same plan running slower.

questions.q: What is the blind spot in SQL Server's default auto-update-statistics behavior?
options: It's reactive — it only fires after a threshold of row changes has already accumulated, and with ASYNC enabled the query that triggers the update still runs against the old statistics
Auto-update statistics runs continuously in real time with zero delay
Auto-update statistics is disabled by default in every SQL Server database
Auto-update statistics only works on Azure SQL Database, never on Managed Instance or on-prem
questions.explain: The threshold-based, reactive nature means some queries can run against stale statistics before the trigger fires, and ASYNC doesn't make the triggering query wait for the refresh.

questions.q: Why would a DBA run UPDATE STATISTICS ... WITH FULLSCAN manually ahead of a known bulk load, instead of trusting auto-update?
options: Because auto-update only fires reactively after enough changes accumulate, so queries right after the load would run on statistics that haven't caught up to the load's new data distribution yet
Because FULLSCAN is required before any INSERT statement will succeed
Because auto-update statistics is permanently disabled on any table larger than 1GB
Because manual updates are always faster than sampled auto-updates
questions.explain: Updating manually as a deliberate maintenance step avoids the gap where post-load queries would otherwise run against pre-load statistics.

questions.q: What does DBCC SHOW_STATISTICS ('table', 'index') WITH STAT_HEADER let a DBA quickly confirm?
options: Whether a suspected bad plan is actually a statistics problem, by showing the Rows, Rows Sampled, and Updated columns
Whether the underlying table has any physical corruption
The exact CPU time a specific query consumed
Whether SQL Server Agent jobs are currently running
questions.explain: The Updated column is the fastest way to check staleness before investigating anything else about a suspect plan.
